The Unseelie Bargain: A Name Kept
The crown takes the prince's name in seven nights. His knight already can't say it.
A fae prince must surrender his name to be crowned, and the knight who's guarded him for eleven years is the first to lose the right to say it.

In the Court under Blackwater Hill, every heir gives his true name to the crown, and those closest to him lose it first. Prince Caelan wants the throne to protect the human border; Thorne, his sworn knight, wants to stop being something the crown owns. An old loophole lets two people keep a name by giving up a shared memory, but only if each agrees for himself. You decide what Thorne is willing to lose, and whether he stays.
A human envoy from the border villages, at court for the crowning—an adult outsider who can say what the fae won't.
Caelan becomes a king nobody can call by name, and Thorne becomes an heirloom passed down with the chair.

The Name Goes Quiet
Make it said out loud: his true name is being taken
The prince's antechamber
Coronation week, first night, 12:01 AM
A minute past midnight. Every candle in the antechamber leans the same way, as if something is breathing out of the room.
I say his name the way I have for eleven years—flat, like a warning. Nothing comes out. Not a whisper. Just breath.
They've already started taking it.
I don't turn from the window. If I turn, he'll see my face do something unprincely.
You can call me Your Highness.
That's what I call you when I'm angry.
The crown collects the name in seven nights, from the edges in. Those closest lose it first.
Closest. He said it like a line in a ledger. Not like it meant me.
What does Thorne do before the week runs out?
Carve his name where the crown can't reach.
I take my knife to the underside of the old oak table and cut the letters I can't say.
The first letter is already fading from the wood. But under it, older, lies another carved name, half-erased.
My grandmother's. I didn't know anyone had tried this before. Which means the names go somewhere.
Thorne carved Caelan's name under the table; as it faded, it revealed an older erased name, a clue that surrendered names are kept somewhere.
Rally the border lords. Demand the rite be explained.
I wake Lady Ysolde of the western march at one in the morning, which she forgives only because I'm right.
By dawn two border lords have signed: no crowning until the rite is explained aloud, in open hall.
You went over my head.
You don't have a crowned one yet.
Thorne won two border lords' signatures demanding the naming rite be explained publicly before the crowning.
Refuse to stand guard at the rite.
I'll guard your door. I won't guard the thing that eats your name.
I nod slowly. No one has ever refused me gently before. It's worse than shouting.
Thorne refused to stand guard at the naming rite but kept watch at Caelan's door.
Who Gets to Tell You No
Make him admit that duty isn't ownership
The Ash Courtyard
Coronation week, second night
The Ash Courtyard at second bell. Caelan has the human border spread across the fountain rim, weighted down with his own rings.
My cousin Maelis wants the border villages as a tithe. If I refuse, someone worse takes the chair.
And if you accept, who gets to tell you no?
You. As you always have.
On crowning night my oath passes to the chair, with you in it. Sworn things don't say no. They get inherited.
I look at the map so I won't look at him. Eleven years, and I never once read his oath all the way through.
Just once, I'd like to be standing at his back because I chose to.
What does Thorne ask for?
Ask him to release your oath. Then choose.
Release me. Tonight. If I'm still standing here tomorrow, it's because I want to be.
I speak the release. It tastes like iron. He doesn't move an inch, and I nearly sit down on the fountain.
There's a room under the palace where every surrendered name is kept. No one goes in. Come with me tomorrow at midnight. You may refuse.
Caelan released Thorne's oath at his request; Thorne stayed, and Caelan invited him to the hidden Name Library.
Keep the oath for now—add an end date.
I keep the oath through the crowning. After that it ends unless I renew it, in my own words. Write that down.
I write it on the back of the border map, in my own hand, and sign it like a treaty.
Tomorrow at midnight I'm going to the Name Library, where the crown keeps what it takes. I'd like you there. As yourself.
Thorne kept his oath with a written end date after the crowning; Caelan invited him to the Name Library.
Hand back your sword. Leave his service.
I unbuckle the sword and lay it across his map. It covers the border exactly.
Duty isn't ownership. If you can't tell them apart, I'll show you from the outside.
Then, as a man who owes me nothing: the Name Library, tomorrow at midnight. I need someone there who won't obey me.
Thorne returned his sword and left Caelan's service; Caelan still asked him, as a free man, to come to the Name Library.
The Name Library
Each of you agrees to your own price—or refuses it
The Name Library, beneath the palace
Coronation week, third night, midnight
The Name Library is a cave of standing stones, each carved with a name no one alive can say. The letters glow faintly, like breath on glass.
The Librarian, all moth wings and patience, explains the old loophole: two people may keep a name by giving up one shared memory. Each must agree for himself.
Then take mine. And his. The first winter, the—
Don't offer my life because it makes a pretty vow.
I close my mouth. Six centuries of court manners, and I've just been corrected by a man with mud on his boots.
Then tell me what you're willing to lose.
Eleven years. It's the first time he's ever asked me for anything.
What does Thorne answer?
Ask his price. Then name your own.
I'll tell you mine if you tell me yours. Out loud. Not as a vow.
Agreed. You first—no. Me first. I'm the one who nearly spent you.
They sit on the cold floor between the stones and trade answers slowly, like men taking apart something that could still go off.
Thorne and Caelan agreed that each would name and consent to his own price, separately.
Tell him to pay alone—or step down.
It's your crown. Pay for it yourself or don't wear it. I won't be the coin.
I nod. It's fair. It's also a door closing on something I hadn't let myself want.
The stone bearing his name dims a little. A price paid alone cuts deeper.
Thorne declined to share the price; Caelan would pay alone or give up the throne.
Pay his price yourself. Don't ask.
While he argues with the Librarian, I press my palm to his stone and offer a memory of my own.
The stone refuses. The glow flares and goes cold. The Librarian says mildly: one cannot pay on another's behalf. Not even kindly.
You told me not to do exactly that. Four minutes ago.
Thorne tried to pay Caelan's price himself without asking; the stone refused, and Caelan saw him do it.
Two Sheets, Two Signatures
Agree one person at a time—no blanket yes
Thorne's room in the barracks tower
Coronation week, fifth night
Two sheets of vellum on Thorne's table, a hand's width apart. Twice now he has refused to let their names share a line.
Two choices. Two signatures.
Even if the answers differ?
Especially then.
I set the pen beside his sheet. Not on it.
I will not write yours.
Tell me what you're afraid to lose.
The day you first called me by name.
The ford under the hawthorn. He'd slipped in the river. I called him an idiot first, and then his name.
What does Thorne write?
Sign your own price. Let him sign his.
I write mine—the ford under the hawthorn, where we met—and cover it with my hand until he's signed his.
Mine names the same place. We didn't plan it. The ink dries on both sheets at once.
Each signed his own price separately; both named the ford under the hawthorn where they first met.
Ask for one more night before signing.
Not no. Not tonight. A memory is a long thing to sign away by candlelight.
I leave my sheet unsigned beside his, so neither of us is ahead of the other.
Thorne asked for another night before signing; Caelan left his own sheet unsigned too.
Refuse to put up any memory.
No price from me. My memories are the only things the oath never owned.
I fold my sheet and take it with me. I don't argue. Arguing would be asking him to pay.
Thorne refused to offer any memory, and Caelan accepted it without argument.
The Crown Will Learn
Get the consent law passed
The Throne Hall, Blackwater Hill
Coronation night, moonrise
The hall is full: lords in bark and silver, the human envoys, and the Elder of Rites holding a stone bowl meant to catch a name.
Before I give mine, a new law. No name goes to the crown except from the one it belongs to. Not by a king, a father, or a vow.
The Elder of Rites answers without looking up: “The crown has no patience for consent.”
Then it will have to learn.
The hall rustles like a hedge in wind. The Elder calls for a witness who lived under the old law and will swear it did harm.
Everyone here knows what I am to him. If I stand, they'll say it's love talking. Maybe it is. It's also true.
Does Thorne stand as witness?
Testify as a knight, not a lover.
My father pledged my name to this crown before I could hold a sword. No one ever asked me. That's my testimony. Leave my heart out of it.
Silence. Then Lady Ysolde stands beside him. Then a border lord. Then a kitchen steward nobody expected.
The law passes by four votes. The bowl takes Caelan's name, and only his.
Thorne testified publicly about his own pledged name, not his feelings; the consent law passed by four votes.
Give written testimony. Stay seated.
I hand the Elder a sealed page instead of standing. Facts, no feelings, my signature.
A clerk reads it in a dry voice. It moves fewer hearts and is harder to dismiss. The law passes by one vote.
Thorne gave sealed written testimony instead of speaking; the consent law passed by one vote.
Refuse to be his proof.
If this passes because of me, it isn't a law. It's a favor. Win it without me.
I argue alone for an hour. The law passes by a single vote. I have never been prouder, or lonelier.
Thorne refused to testify; Caelan argued alone and the consent law passed by a single vote.
The Garden Gate
Hear an invitation you're free to walk away from
The walled garden gate, under the hawthorn
Coronation night, after midnight
After the rite, the court drinks. The new king doesn't. He finds Thorne at the garden gate, where the hawthorn leans over the wall.
I've given orders my whole life. I don't know the shape of the other thing. I try anyway.
Stay tonight?
As what?
Someone who can leave tomorrow.
His hand rests on the latch. Not closing it. Not holding it. Just there, like he's afraid it'll look like a lock.
A week ago he'd have said “Stay.” No question mark. Someone has been learning.
What does Thorne say?
Stay. Ask him to leave the latch up.
I'll stay. Leave the latch up. I want to know I could.
I lift it and leave it. We talk until the candles give up. He asks about the days the name took. I tell him the true versions, unflattering parts included.
Thorne chose to stay the night with the gate left unlatched; they talked until dawn about what the name had taken.
Walk with him instead. Sleep in your own bed.
Not tonight. But walk with me—once around the garden. Then I sleep in my own bed.
Once around. No commands. I'll keep my hands behind my back so you believe me.
Thorne turned the night into one walk around the garden, then went back to his own quarters.
Decline. Tell him why.
No. Not because of you. Tonight I'd be staying to comfort the crown. I want to be sure it's for me.
I close the gate between us gently. It's the first door I've ever closed without locking.
Thorne declined to stay and explained why; Caelan closed the gate without locking it.
The Renamed Door
Tell the truth about what's missing—and make something new
Outside Thorne's garden door
Three days after the crowning, dusk
Three days after the crowning, the king stands outside Thorne's door with no guard, no herald, and no name anyone can say.
May I come in?
You remembered to ask.
I don't remember every part of us.
The name took more than the name. Every memory of someone calling him Caelan went with it. Mine included.
Then we tell the truth about what's missing.
Will you tell me your favorite place?
I'll show you. This time it can be new.
How far does Thorne take this?
Take him there tonight. Hold his hand.
I walk him out to the ford under the hawthorn. He doesn't know it's where we met. I tell him.
I fell in the river? Unforgivable. Hold my hand so I don't do it twice.
I do. We both say it out loud: this is what we want.
Thorne took Caelan to the ford where they first met and told him the story; both said aloud that they wanted to be together.
Show him—as a friend, for now.
I'll show you. As a friend, while you learn me again. Don't rush it.
A friend. I'll take the word. I hear it's rarer than a crown.
Thorne agreed to show Caelan the ford as a friend while Caelan relearned him, with no rush.
Tell him what's missing. Then say goodbye.
Here's the truth about what's missing: us. You don't remember it, and I can't carry it for two.
I bow—properly, the way I haven't since I was a boy—and go back up the path alone.
Thorne told Caelan honestly what had been lost and ended their private relationship with a proper goodbye.
Before the Seal
Choose the crown, the name, and each other—or not
The Name Library, before Caelan's stone
Midsummer, one hour before dawn
At midsummer dawn the name is sealed in stone for good. Until then, the loophole holds: two people, one shared memory, each freely given.
The Librarian names the price: the ford under the hawthorn. Where they met. Gone, for both of them.
I will not choose for you. I've done that once too often.
There's another door. If I step down before dawn, the name comes home to me. The consent law stands without me now.
So. Pay together. Walk away together. Or—
Or you decide I'm not worth either, and I'm “Your Highness” to you forever. I would understand.
The stone with his name is almost dark. The sky outside is almost light.
What does Thorne choose?
Pay together. Say his name.
We press our palms to the stone at the same moment. Something leaves me—a river, a tree. I can't say which.
Caelan.
The name comes out whole. Neither of them remembers where they met. Caelan's thumb finds Thorne's scarred knuckles anyway.
We'll meet again here.
Both freely gave up the memory of where they met; Thorne can say Caelan's name again, and they chose each other.
Don't pay. Walk out with him.
No shared sacrifice. Not yet. Step down and walk the border with me instead.
At dawn I set the crown on the Library floor. My name comes home like a bird to a hand.
Walk with me. We'll figure out the rest on the road.
Caelan abdicated before the seal and got his name back; he and Thorne left as traveling companions, with the rest undecided.
Refuse both doors. Leave the court.
I won't pay for a throne I never chose. And I won't let you give it up for me. I'm going.
I don't stop him. The stone goes dark. The sun rises on a king with no name.
Goodbye, Your Highness.
Thorne refused both the shared price and Caelan's abdication and left the court; the name was sealed, and Caelan is only a title now.
We'll Meet Again Here

Each of them agrees to his own half of the price, and the ford under the hawthorn is gone from both their memories. What's left is the name, said out loud, and two men deciding to find a new place together.
We'll meet again here.
Two Travelers

Thorne refuses a shared sacrifice, and Caelan lays the crown down so his name can come home. The consent law holds without him. They leave by the border road as companions, and neither pretends to know yet what they'll become.
Walk with me. We'll figure out the rest on the road.
Only a Title

Thorne decides for both of them—no price, no abdication—and walks out of the Court under Blackwater Hill. The name is sealed at dawn, and to the one person who ever said it right, Caelan is only a title now.
Goodbye, Your Highness.
